decks.title: Sectors of the Indian Economy — Part 1: Sectors, GDP and Employment
goals: Classify economic activities into the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors and explain how they depend on each other
Explain GDP and why only final goods and services are counted
Interpret how the shares of the sectors in output and employment have changed, in developed countries and in India
Explain disguised unemployment and underemployment, and ways to create more employment, including MGNREGA 2005

slides.heading: Sectors of the Indian Economy
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **three sectors**, **GDP**, how their importance changes, **disguised unemployment** and **MGNREGA**.

nodes.label: How they depend on each other

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: three sectors, interdependence, GDP, changing importance, hidden unemployment, creating jobs and MGNREGA
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! Think of your breakfast this morning. Someone grew the wheat, someone turned it into bread, and someone carried it to the shop and sold it. Each of these people did a different kind of work. In this chapter we group all such work into three sectors, see how we measure what a country produces, and ask an important question: are there enough good jobs for everyone?

slides.heading: Economic activities
slides.body_md: An **economic activity** produces a good or a service in exchange for money (or for one's own use).

rows: A farmer near Nashik grows onions
A factory in Kolkata bakes biscuits
A teacher in Imphal teaches Class 10

visual.alt: Table of three activities: growing vegetables produces a good from nature, making biscuits produces a good by manufacturing, and teaching produces a service

slides.narration: An economic activity is any work that produces a good or a service, usually in return for money. Notice the three kinds of work in this table. The onion farmer takes a good directly from nature. The biscuit factory changes wheat, sugar and oil into a new product. The teacher does not make any object at all; she provides a service. These three kinds of work are the basis of the three sectors.

slides.heading: The three sectors

rows: Produces goods by using natural resources directly
Changes natural products into other forms by manufacturing
Sugar mill, textile mill, furniture workshop, bakery
Provides services that support production and people's needs
Transport, storage, banking, trade, teaching, health care, IT

visual.alt: Table of the three sectors: primary uses natural resources directly (farming, fishing, dairy, forestry); secondary manufactures (sugar mill, textile mill, furniture, bakery); tertiary provides services (transport, storage, banking, trade, teaching, health, IT)

slides.narration: Here is the main classification. The primary sector uses natural resources directly: farming, fishing, dairy and forestry. Because most of its products come from agriculture, it is also called the agriculture and related sector. The secondary sector changes natural products into other forms by manufacturing, so it is also called the industrial sector. The tertiary sector provides services such as transport, banking, trade, teaching and health care, so it is called the service sector.

slides.heading: Quick check: which sector?
slides.body_md: Which one of these is a **secondary**-sector activity?
slides.narration: Ask yourself one question for each option: is nature used directly, is a product being changed into another form, or is a service being provided?

slides.heading: One product, three sectors

nodes.label: Dairy plant makes paneer and ghee (secondary)
Trucks, shops and banks move, sell and finance them (tertiary)

visual.alt: Flow showing one product across the sectors: a dairy farmer (primary), a dairy plant making paneer and ghee (secondary), trucks, shops and banks (tertiary), and a family buying paneer
visual.caption: One product, three sectors

slides.narration: Follow a glass of milk. The dairy farmer works in the primary sector. The dairy plant that turns milk into paneer and ghee is in the secondary sector. The trucks that carry it, the shop that sells it and the bank that lends to the dairy are all in the tertiary sector. So one product passes through all three sectors before it reaches your plate.

slides.heading: The sectors depend on each other
slides.body_md: A problem in one sector spreads to the others.

nodes.label: Truckers, traders and banks lose business (tertiary)

visual.alt: Flow of a chain of effects: a cotton crop failure leads to less raw cotton for mills, less business for truckers, traders and banks, and lower incomes across the economy
visual.caption: Interdependence works in both directions

slides.narration: Because one product passes through all three sectors, they depend on each other. Suppose the cotton crop fails. Mills get less raw cotton and may cut production. Truck owners, traders and banks lose business too. It works the other way as well: if mills stop buying, cotton farmers suffer. This is called interdependence, and examiners love to ask for an example of it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classifying activities
slides.body_md: Classify six activities in an imagined village in Kerala, with a reason for each.
bullets: Step 1 — Ask: is a natural resource used directly? Then it is **primary**.
Step 2 — Is a product changed into another form? Then it is **secondary**.
Step 3 — Is a service provided (transport, repair, teaching, trade)? Then it is **tertiary**.
Step 4 — Write the sector **and** the reason; the reason earns the mark.

rows: A teacher at the village school

visual.alt: Table classifying six activities in an imagined Kerala village: tapping rubber and catching sardines are primary; making rubber sheets and tyres is secondary; transport, teaching and boat repair are tertiary
visual.caption: Ask: does it use nature directly, change a product, or provide a service?

slides.narration: Let us practise with an imagined village in Kerala. Tapping rubber trees and catching fish use nature directly, so they are primary. Turning latex into rubber sheets and tyres is manufacturing, so it is secondary. Carrying sheets to Kochi, teaching, and repairing boats are services, so they are tertiary. Notice the boat-repair yard: repair is a service, even though it happens in a workshop.

slides.heading: Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
slides.body_md: **GDP** = the value of all **final** goods and services produced **within a country** during a particular year.
bullets: **Final goods** reach the consumer, e.g. bread, a bicycle, a haircut.
**Intermediate goods** are used up in making other goods, e.g. flour used by a bakery.
Only final goods are counted: their price **already includes** the intermediate goods.
In India, GDP is estimated by the **National Statistics Office** of the central government's statistics ministry.

nodes.label: Final goods and services (bread, cycles, shirts, haircuts)

visual.alt: Flow: intermediate goods such as flour, steel and yarn are used up in production; final goods and services are what GDP counts
visual.caption: Count final goods only

slides.narration: To compare the sectors, economists add up the value of what each sector produces. The total for the country is the Gross Domestic Product, or GDP. The key word is final. A bakery buys flour and sells bread. If we counted the flour and the bread, the flour would be counted twice, because its value is already inside the price of the bread. So GDP counts only final goods and services.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: avoiding double counting
slides.body_md: Wheat worth ₹800 → flour worth ₹1,200 → bread worth ₹2,000 (imagined). How much is added to GDP?
bullets: Step 1 — Identify the final good: the **bread** sold to consumers.
Step 2 — Count it once: **₹2,000**.
Step 3 — Check with value added: 800 + 400 + 800 = **₹2,000**.
Step 4 — Wrong method: 800 + 1,200 + 2,000 = ₹4,000 counts wheat and flour twice.

visual.alt: Table of a wheat–flour–bread chain: wheat sold for 800 rupees, flour for 1,200 and bread for 2,000; values added are 800, 400 and 800; only the final good worth 2,000 is counted, which equals the total value added
visual.caption: Imagined figures.

slides.narration: Here is the classic trap. The tempting answer adds all three sales and gets four thousand rupees. But the wheat is inside the flour, and the flour is inside the bread. The correct answer is two thousand rupees, the value of the final bread. As a check, add only the value each stage adds: eight hundred, then four hundred, then eight hundred. That also gives two thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: GDP
slides.body_md: True or false? The value of the flour bought by a bakery is added to GDP separately from the bread it sells.
slides.narration: Remember the bakery example. Is the flour a final good or an intermediate good?

slides.heading: How the sectors changed in developed countries

visual.alt: Line chart of an imagined developed country from 1800 to 2000: the primary share of workers falls from 75 to 5 per cent, the secondary share rises to 40 per cent by 1900 and then falls to 22, and the tertiary share rises from 15 to 73 per cent
visual.caption: Imagined developed country: primary → secondary → tertiary.

slides.narration: This chart shows an imagined developed country over two hundred years. At first most people farmed, herded or fished. As farming improved, fewer farmers could feed everyone, and people moved into crafts and then factories, so the secondary sector grew. In the twentieth century services took over, and today most workers there are in the tertiary sector. Primary, then secondary, then tertiary: remember that order.

slides.heading: India: output has shifted, jobs have not
slides.body_md: Rounded, approximate shares for recent years.

x.label: Bars 1–3: share of GDP; bars 5–7: share of workers (primary, secondary, tertiary)

visual.alt: Bar chart for India in recent years, rounded and approximate: share of GDP is about 18 per cent primary, 28 secondary and 54 tertiary; share of workers is about 46 per cent primary, 25 secondary and 29 tertiary
visual.caption: India, recent years (rounded, approximate; exact values change every year).

slides.narration: Now India. Look at the first three bars. The tertiary sector produces more than half of our GDP, and the primary sector less than a fifth. Now look at the last three bars. Close to half of all workers still depend on the primary sector. So production has shifted to services, but jobs have not shifted as much. This mismatch is the central problem of this chapter.

slides.heading: Why has the tertiary sector grown so much?

rows: Hospitals, schools, post offices, police, courts, banks
Transport, storage, trade and credit for crops and factory goods
More eating out, tourism, private schools and hospitals
Software, internet services, digital payments, call centres

visual.alt: Table of four reasons the tertiary sector has grown: basic services, support for other sectors, rising incomes and new technology, each with examples

slides.narration: Why have services grown so fast? First, every country needs basic services like hospitals, schools, police and banks. Second, as farming and industry grow, they need more transport, storage, trade and credit. Third, as incomes rise, people spend more on eating out, travel and private schools. Fourth, new technology has created whole new services, from software to digital payments. But remember: not every service job is well paid.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the pattern
slides.body_md: Which of the statements about India are correct?
slides.narration: Look back at the two sets of bars before you choose. Did jobs move as fast as output?

slides.heading: Hidden unemployment
columns:
**Disguised unemployment (mainly rural)**

- More people work on a task than are needed
- Everyone looks busy
- If some leave, **output does not fall**
- Common on small family farms

**Underemployment (rural and urban)**

- People work below their capacity
- Casual workers get work only some days
- Vendors and repair persons wait for customers
- Income is low and uncertain
slides.narration: If so many people are still in agriculture, are they fully employed? Often not. In disguised unemployment, more people work on a small farm than it needs. Everyone looks busy, but if some left, the harvest would be the same. In cities, many casual workers, painters and vendors find work only some days. Both are kinds of underemployment: people work, but below their capacity.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: measuring disguised unemployment
slides.body_md: An imagined family in Bihar: seven members work on a 2-hectare plot. With only four members, output stays at 40 quintals.
bullets: Step 1 — Workers really needed: **4**.
Step 2 — Surplus: 7 − 4 = **3**.
Step 3 — Test: output with 7 = output with 4, so the 3 add nothing.
Step 4 — Conclude: **3 members are disguisedly unemployed**; they could earn elsewhere without lowering farm output.

rows: All family members work on the 2-hectare plot
Only four members work on the plot

visual.alt: Table: with seven members working, output is 40 quintals; with four, it is still 40 quintals; so three members are disguisedly unemployed
visual.caption: Imagined figures.

slides.narration: Let us measure it. Seven family members produce forty quintals of paddy. When only four work, the plot still produces forty quintals. So three members are not really adding anything. They are disguisedly unemployed. The good news is hidden in the answer: if these three found work in a nearby mill or shop, the family's farm output would not fall, and its total income would rise.

slides.heading: How can more jobs be created?

nodes.label: More jobs in and near villages
Tourism, health, education and IT services

visual.alt: Flow from one goal, more jobs in and near villages, to five ways: irrigation for a second crop; roads, transport and cold storage; cheap credit; agro-processing units; and tourism, health, education and IT services
visual.caption: Ways to create employment

slides.narration: So how do we create more work? Irrigation lets farmers grow a second crop, so they need labour for more months. Roads and cold storage let produce reach bigger markets, creating jobs in transport and trade. Cheap credit helps people start small enterprises. Food-processing units in small towns use local crops. And services like tourism, health, education and IT can employ many more people, especially if they are trained.

slides.heading: MGNREGA 2005: the right to work
slides.body_md: The **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act**, 2005. *Update: in December 2025 Parliament passed a new law to replace it with a rural job guarantee of 125 days; your 2026–27 syllabus still names MGNREGA 2005, so learn its features.*

rows: Every rural household whose adults volunteer for unskilled manual work can demand it
Work must be given within 15 days of applying, or an unemployment allowance is due
At least one-third of the workers should be women
Water conservation, ponds, check dams, land development, tree planting, rural roads
Wages into bank or post-office accounts; social audits by the gram sabha

visual.alt: Table of five features of MGNREGA 2005: 100 days a year for rural households, work within 15 days or an allowance, at least one-third women, works such as water conservation and rural roads, and wages paid into accounts with social audits

slides.narration: To deal with rural unemployment, Parliament passed MGNREGA in 2005. It guarantees one hundred days of unskilled manual work a year to every rural household that asks. If work is not given within fifteen days, the household gets an unemployment allowance. At least one third of the workers should be women. The works, like ponds and check dams, are chosen to raise future farm output. In December 2025 a new law was passed to replace it, but learn the 2005 Act for your exam.

slides.heading: Quick check: MGNREGA
slides.body_md: If work is not given within 15 days of an application under MGNREGA, what happens?
slides.narration: Remember why the Act is called a right to work. What does the law promise if the government does not keep its side?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Value of final goods and services produced within a country in a year; no double counting
Tertiary produces over half of GDP, but the primary sector still employs the most workers
More workers than needed; removing some does not reduce output
100 days of work for rural households; allowance if not given in 15 days

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: three sectors, GDP, change over time, India's pattern, disguised unemployment and MGNREGA 2005

slides.narration: Here is Part 1 in a nutshell. Work is grouped into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors, and they depend on each other. GDP adds up final goods and services, never the intermediate ones. Developed countries moved from primary to secondary to tertiary. In India, services now produce over half of GDP, but agriculture still employs the most people, many of them underemployed. MGNREGA gives rural households a legal right to one hundred days of work.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Classify by the **nature of the activity** and give the reason; repair, transport and trade are tertiary.
GDP: write **final**, **within a country**, **one year**; mention double counting.
Data questions: compare **output share and employment share** for each sector, quoting figures.
Disguised unemployment: always add "**output does not fall** if some workers leave".
MGNREGA: **100 days**, **rural households**, **15 days or allowance**, **one-third women**.
Interdependence: give a **chain** through all three sectors, not a list.
slides.narration: Some tips. When you classify an activity, the reason earns the mark, so always write it. In a GDP answer, three words matter: final, within a country, and one year. In data questions, compare both columns, output and jobs, with numbers. For disguised unemployment, never forget the test: output does not fall. And for MGNREGA, four numbers and words win marks: one hundred days, rural households, fifteen days, one third women.

decks.title: Sectors of the Indian Economy — Part 2: Organised and Unorganised, Public and Private
goals: Compare the organised and unorganised sectors and explain how unorganised workers can be protected
Distinguish the public and private sectors by ownership and motive
Explain why the government provides some goods and services itself

slides.heading: Two more ways to classify work
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **organised vs unorganised** (conditions of work) and **public vs private** (ownership).

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: conditions of work, organised and unorganised sectors, protecting workers, ownership, public and private sectors, and the role of government
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 1 we classified work by what people do. Now we use two other lenses. The first asks: what are the conditions of work? Is the job regular and protected, or not? That gives the organised and unorganised sectors. The second asks: who owns the enterprise, the government or private persons? That gives the public and private sectors. One worker can belong to several classifications at once.

slides.heading: The organised sector
slides.body_md: Enterprises or places of work where the **terms of employment are regular** and people have **assured work**.

headers: What it means for a worker
rows: The enterprise must follow labour laws
Job and terms are written down
Paid leave, provident fund, medical benefits, pension
Protection in illness and old age

visual.alt: Table of four features of the organised sector and what each means for a worker: registration, appointment letter, fixed hours with overtime pay, and paid leave, provident fund, medical benefits and pension

slides.narration: The organised sector covers enterprises that are registered with the government and must follow its rules on employment. A worker gets an appointment letter, works fixed hours and is paid extra for overtime. She gets paid leave, provident fund, medical benefits and, often, a pension. Many of these rules were brought together in four labour codes that came into force in November 2025. Such jobs are regular and secure.

slides.heading: The unorganised sector
slides.body_md: Small and scattered units, largely **outside government control**; rules exist but are **not followed**.

headers: Who works in the unorganised sector
rows: Landless farm labourers, small and marginal farmers, sharecroppers, artisans such as weavers and carpenters
Construction workers, street vendors, head-load workers, domestic workers, workers in small workshops
App-based delivery and ride-hailing workers paid per task

visual.alt: Table of who works in the unorganised sector: in rural areas landless labourers, small farmers, sharecroppers and artisans; in urban areas construction workers, vendors, head-load and domestic workers; and new app-based delivery and ride workers

slides.narration: The unorganised sector is made up of small, scattered units, often not registered. Rules may exist, but they are not followed. Jobs are low-paid and irregular, and a worker can be told to leave at any time. Look at who works here: landless labourers, small farmers, artisans, construction and domestic workers, vendors, and now many app-based delivery riders. Together, they make up a large majority of India's workers.

slides.heading: Comparing the two
columns:
**Organised**

- Registered; labour laws followed
- Regular job, appointment letter
- Paid leave, provident fund, pension
- Fixed hours, overtime pay

**Unorganised**

- Small, scattered; rules not followed
- Irregular work; dismissal any time
- No paid leave or benefits
- Long hours, low pay
slides.narration: Put the two side by side. Notice that every point has a pair: registered versus not, regular versus irregular, benefits versus none, fixed hours versus long hours. In the exam, a difference earns its mark only when you state both sides. Writing only that organised jobs are secure is half an answer; add that unorganised workers can be dismissed at any time.

slides.heading: Quick check: organised sector
slides.body_md: Which of these is a feature of the **organised** sector?
slides.narration: Three options describe one sector and one describes the other. Which one is about protection for workers?

slides.heading: Unorganised work inside big companies

nodes.label: No paid leave, provident fund or security

visual.alt: Flow: big firms hire through contractors, workers are on short contracts, they get no paid leave, provident fund or security, so unorganised conditions spread inside organised firms
visual.caption: A trend since the 1990s

slides.narration: Here is a trend worth knowing. Since the nineteen nineties, many large companies have hired workers through contractors on short contracts instead of as permanent staff. These workers may work in a big, registered factory or office, but they get no paid leave, provident fund or security. So unorganised conditions have spread even inside the organised sector. The size of the employer does not decide the sector; the terms of work do.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: organised or unorganised?
slides.body_md: Classify five imagined workers.
bullets: Step 1 — Look for the clues: appointment letter, salary, paid leave, provident fund.
Step 2 — If they are present, the job is **organised**.
Step 3 — If pay is per piece, per day or per task with no benefits, it is **unorganised**.
Step 4 — Ignore how big or famous the employer is.

rows: Nurse in a government hospital, Patna
Woman rolling agarbattis at home for a trader, Mysuru
Paid per thousand sticks, no benefits
Engineer in a registered software company, Pune
Regular salary, provident fund, health cover
Security guard hired through a contractor for a bank
Taxi driver working through an app, Kolkata
Paid per ride, no fixed salary

visual.alt: Table classifying five imagined workers: a government nurse and a software engineer are organised; an agarbatti roller at home, a contract security guard and an app-based taxi driver are unorganised, with clues for each
visual.caption: Look at the terms of work, not the size or fame of the employer.

slides.narration: Let us practise. The government nurse and the software engineer have regular salaries and benefits, so they are organised. The woman rolling agarbattis at home is paid per thousand sticks, with nothing else, so she is unorganised. The security guard works in a bank, but through a contractor without leave or security, so he is unorganised too. And the app-based driver, paid per ride, is unorganised.

slides.heading: Protecting unorganised workers

rows: Enforce minimum wages; simple ways to complain
No help in illness, injury or old age
Social security: health and accident cover, pensions; registration on the e-Shram portal
Small units cannot get credit or markets
Cheap loans, raw materials and marketing support; cooperatives
Skill training linked to local work

visual.alt: Table of problems of unorganised workers and measures: minimum wages for low pay, social security and e-Shram registration for illness and old age, credit and marketing support for small units, and skill training

slides.narration: How can these workers be protected? Minimum wages must actually be paid. Social security matters most: health and accident cover and pensions, which the government now reaches through registration on the e-Shram portal, where more than thirty crore workers have registered. Small units need cheap credit, raw materials and help with marketing. Cooperatives and skill training raise incomes too. Protection is needed on economic grounds, and also on social grounds.

slides.heading: Quick check: a new kind of job
slides.body_md: Ayaan delivers food in Pune through an app, paid per delivery, with no paid leave. Which sector is his work closest to?
slides.narration: Remember the last two slides. Do the size and fame of the app company decide the sector, or do the terms of work?

slides.heading: Public and private sectors

rows: Individuals or companies own the assets
Indian Railways, India Post, government hospitals
A private airline, a mobile phone company, a private school

visual.alt: Table comparing public and private sectors by ownership, motive, source of money and examples: Indian Railways, India Post and government hospitals versus a private airline, a mobile company and a private school

slides.narration: Now the second lens: ownership. In the public sector, the government owns most of the assets and provides the services, like Indian Railways, India Post or a government hospital. In the private sector, individuals or companies own the assets. The motives differ too. A private firm must earn a profit to survive. The public sector aims at public welfare, and may run some services even at a loss.

slides.heading: Why the government provides some things

headers: Why the private sector alone would not
rows: Huge cost; hard to charge every user enough for a profit
A profit-seeking firm would charge the full cost
Grain bought at a support price, sold cheaply in ration shops
Helps farmers and the poor; no profit in it
Many poor families cannot pay private prices

visual.alt: Table of what the government provides and why: infrastructure because of huge cost, cheap electricity, grain procurement and ration shops, and schools and hospitals for families who cannot pay private prices

slides.narration: Why can we not leave everything to private firms? Some things, like roads, bridges and dams, need huge spending, and it is hard to charge each user enough to make a profit. Some things, like cheap electricity for small industries, help development but would not pay a private firm. And many families cannot afford private prices for schools, hospitals and food. So the government steps in, paying for it from taxes.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: why ration shops exist
slides.body_md: Explain how and why the government supplies cheap foodgrains.
bullets: Step 1 — The Food Corporation of India buys wheat and rice from farmers at a **minimum support price**.
Step 2 — It **stores** the grain and sends it to **ration shops**.
Step 3 — Eligible families get it **cheaply or free**; about 80 crore people are covered.
Step 4 — Why public? It supports **farmers** and gives the **poor** food security; the government bears the cost, so there is no profit in it.

nodes.label: Farmers sell grain at a minimum support price
Food Corporation of India buys and stores it
Ration shops sell it cheaply or give it free

visual.alt: Flow: farmers sell grain at a minimum support price, the Food Corporation of India buys and stores it, ration shops sell it cheaply or give it free, and poor families get food security
visual.caption: The government bears the difference in cost.

slides.narration: Here is the public sector in action. The Food Corporation of India buys grain from farmers at a minimum support price, which protects farm incomes. It stores the grain and sends it to ration shops, where eligible families get it cheaply or free. The government pays the difference. No private trader would do this, because there is no profit in it. The motive is welfare.

slides.heading: Quick check: ration shops
slides.body_md: Why does the government buy grain at a support price and sell it cheaply through ration shops?
slides.narration: Think about the motive of the public sector. Is it profit, or something else?

slides.heading: Worked example 3: planning a five-mark comparison
slides.body_md: *Distinguish between the organised and unorganised sectors on any five points.*
bullets: Step 1 — Choose five **bases**: registration, rules, security, benefits, hours and pay.
Step 2 — For each base, write **both** sectors in one numbered point.
Step 3 — Bold the key words examiners look for.
Step 4 — Stay within about 120 words; five numbered points, one mark each.

visual.alt: Answer plan table for a five-mark comparison: registration, rules, security, benefits, and hours and pay, each stated for both sectors
visual.caption: One mark per point; every point names both sectors.

slides.narration: A five-mark comparison is easy to plan. Choose five bases, like registration, rules, security, benefits, and hours and pay. Then write one numbered point for each base, always stating both sectors. A table in your head turns into five clean sentences. This plan also works for public versus private sectors: ownership, motive, source of money, examples and the kind of services provided.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Registered, follows labour laws, regular jobs with benefits
Small, scattered, rules not followed, insecure and low-paid
Minimum wages, social security (e-Shram), support to small units
Government owns; aims at welfare (railways, post, ration shops)
Huge-cost infrastructure, support to producers, health, education, food

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: organised and unorganised sectors, protection of workers, public and private sectors, and why the government provides some goods and services

slides.narration: Here is Part 2 in brief. The organised sector is registered, follows labour laws and gives regular jobs with benefits. The unorganised sector is small and scattered, with insecure, low-paid work, and it employs most Indian workers, so protecting them matters. The public sector is owned by the government and aims at welfare; the private sector is privately owned and aims at profit. The government provides what private firms would not.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Organised vs unorganised = **conditions of work**; public vs private = **ownership**.
In a difference question, state **both sectors** in every point.
Contract workers in big firms have **unorganised** conditions.
Public sector motive = **welfare**, not only profit; give an example (railways, ration shops).
For "protect unorganised workers", cover **wages, social security and support to small units**.
One person can be in several classes: a nurse in a government hospital is tertiary, organised and public.
slides.narration: Final tips. Keep the bases of classification clear: organised and unorganised are about conditions of work; public and private are about ownership; primary, secondary and tertiary are about the nature of work. One person can belong to all three at once. In difference questions, write both sides of every point. And for protection of workers, cover wages, social security and support for small enterprises.

notes.title: Sectors of the Indian Economy — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Primary, secondary and tertiary sectors
sections.body_md:
Economic activities are grouped by the **nature of the activity**.

- **Primary sector:** goods produced by **using natural resources directly**: farming, dairy, fishing, forestry. Also called the **agriculture and related sector**.
- **Secondary sector:** natural products **changed into other forms** by manufacturing: sugar from cane, cloth from cotton, furniture from wood. Also called the **industrial sector**.
- **Tertiary sector:** activities that **do not produce a good** but provide **services**: transport, storage, communication, banking, trade, teaching, health care, IT. Also called the **service sector**.

**Interdependence:** the sectors depend on each other. Farmers sell to mills and need transport and credit; mills need raw materials from farms; services earn by moving, selling and financing farm and factory goods. A crop failure, or a factory closure, spreads through all three.

sections.heading: 2. Gross Domestic Product
sections.body_md:
**GDP** is the value of all **final goods and services** produced **within a country** during a **particular year**. Adding the output of the three sectors gives GDP.

- **Final goods** reach the consumer (bread, a bicycle, a haircut).
- **Intermediate goods** are used up in making other goods (flour for a bakery, cotton yarn for a weaver).
- Only final goods are counted, because their price **already includes** the intermediate goods; counting both is **double counting**. Adding the **value added** at each stage gives the same total.

In India, GDP is estimated by the **National Statistics Office** under the central government's Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.

sections.heading: 3. Changing importance of the sectors
sections.body_md:
**Developed countries:** at first most people worked in the primary sector. Better farming freed labour; with new methods, factories spread and the **secondary sector** became most important. Over the last century the **tertiary sector** became the largest in both output and employment.

**India:** over the decades the **tertiary sector** has become the **largest producing sector**; it now produces more than half of GDP, while the primary sector produces less than a fifth. But **employment has not shifted as much**: the primary sector is still the **largest employer**, with a little under half of all workers.

**Why services grew:** basic services (hospitals, schools, police, courts, banks); support for farming and industry (transport, storage, trade, credit); rising incomes (eating out, tourism, private schools and hospitals); and new IT-based services. **But** growth is uneven: alongside well-paid IT and finance jobs are many small shopkeepers, vendors and repair persons who earn little.

sections.heading: 4. Disguised unemployment and underemployment
sections.body_md:
Because jobs have not grown enough outside agriculture, many people remain on farms.

- **Disguised unemployment:** more people work on a task than are needed. All **appear employed**, but if some leave, **output does not fall**. Typical of small family farms.
- **Underemployment:** people work **below their potential**. In cities, casual workers (painters, plumbers, loaders) find work only some days; vendors wait all day for few customers.

The surplus workers could move to other work **without reducing farm output**, so creating such work raises incomes.

sections.heading: 6. Organised and unorganised sectors
sections.body_md:
This classification is based on **conditions of work**.

- **Organised sector:** enterprises **registered** with the government that follow labour laws. Jobs are **regular**, with an appointment letter, fixed hours, overtime pay, **paid leave, provident fund, medical benefits** and often a pension. (Since November 2025 many older labour laws have been merged into **four labour codes**.)
- **Unorganised sector:** **small and scattered** units, largely outside government control; rules are **not followed**. Work is **low-paid, irregular** and insecure; there is no paid leave or provident fund, and workers can be dismissed any time.

**Who:** landless labourers, small farmers, sharecroppers and artisans in villages; construction, domestic and head-load workers, vendors and workers in small workshops in towns; app-based delivery and ride workers paid per task. Workers from socially disadvantaged communities and many women are over-represented. A large majority of India's workers, around nine in ten, work without formal protection.

**Trend:** since the 1990s, more firms hire through **contractors**, so unorganised conditions spread even inside organised enterprises.

**Protection:** enforce **minimum wages**; **social security** (health and accident cover, pensions) through registration on the **e-Shram** portal; cheap credit, raw materials and marketing for small units; cooperatives and skill training.

sections.heading: 7. Public and private sectors
sections.body_md:
This classification is based on **ownership**.

- **Public sector:** the **government owns** most assets and provides the services: Indian Railways, India Post, government schools and hospitals. Aim: **public welfare**.
- **Private sector:** **individuals or companies** own the assets. Aim: **profit**.

**Why the government provides some things:**
1. **Infrastructure** (roads, bridges, railways, ports, dams) needs huge spending, and it is hard to charge every user enough for a profit.
2. **Support to producers:** cheap electricity for small industries; grain bought from farmers at a **minimum support price** by the Food Corporation of India.
3. **Food security:** grain sold cheaply or given free through **ration shops** (about 80 crore people are covered).
4. **Health, education and nutrition** for families who cannot pay private prices.

The money comes mainly from **taxes**.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Classifying by the place of work: a boat-repair workshop is **tertiary** (a service); a potter at home is **secondary**.
- Leaving out "**final**" in the definition of GDP, or adding intermediate goods (double counting).
- Saying the tertiary sector employs the most people in India: it **produces** the most; the **primary** sector **employs** the most.
- Defining disguised unemployment without the test "**output does not fall**".
- Saying MGNREGA covers cities or gives 100 days per person: it is **100 days per rural household**.
- Treating every worker of a big company as organised: **contract workers** are not protected.
- Mixing up the bases: organised/unorganised = conditions of work; public/private = ownership.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark MCQ and assertion-reason: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two points, or a point with an example (about 40 words).
- 3 marks: three distinct points (about 60 words); difference questions state both sides.
- 5 marks: five numbered points (about 120 words); data questions quote figures, interpret them and suggest a remedy.

**Data in SOYL practice** are imagined but realistic; your board paper will give its own table. Compare every row and column before you write.

questions.stem_md: Kavita grows mushrooms in a shed on her farm near Solan and sells them at the weekly market. **Growing** the mushrooms belongs to which sector?

options.text_md: Secondary sector
Primary sector
Tertiary sector
Public sector

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Primary sector. Growing a crop uses natural resources directly (soil, water, organic matter), so it is a primary activity. Selling at the market is trade (tertiary), but the question asks about growing. "Public sector" is about ownership, not the type of activity.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following is a **secondary**-sector activity?

options.text_md: A fisherman catching pomfret off the Konkan coast
A truck carrying milk cans from villages to the dairy
A veterinary doctor treating a sick cow
A cooperative dairy turning milk into paneer and ghee

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A cooperative dairy turning milk into paneer and ghee. The secondary sector changes a natural product into another form by manufacturing: milk becomes paneer and ghee. Fishing is primary; transporting and treating animals are services (tertiary).

questions.stem_md: Why is the tertiary sector also called the **service sector**?

options.text_md: Its activities do not make a good themselves but provide services that support production and people's needs
It produces goods by using natural resources directly
It converts raw materials into finished goods in factories
It is owned and run only by the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Its activities do not make a good themselves but provide services that support production and people's needs. Transport, banking, trade, teaching and health care produce services, not goods. Using natural resources directly describes the primary sector, manufacturing the secondary sector, and ownership has nothing to do with this classification.

questions.stem_md: A drought sharply reduces the cotton crop in an imagined district of Gujarat. Which is the most likely chain of effects?

options.text_md: Only cotton farmers lose; the secondary and tertiary sectors are not affected
Textile mills produce more cloth because there is less cotton to buy
Textile mills get less raw cotton, and the transporters and traders who move and sell cotton earn less
Banks gain because farmers stop borrowing from them

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Textile mills get less raw cotton, and the transporters and traders who move and sell cotton earn less. The sectors are interdependent: a shortfall in the primary sector (cotton) reduces raw material for the secondary sector (mills) and business for the tertiary sector (transport, trade, banking). The other options ignore or reverse these links.

questions.stem_md: Because most natural products come from farming, dairy, fishing and forestry, the primary sector is also called the

options.text_md: industrial sector
service sector
agriculture and related sector
unorganised sector

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** agriculture and related sector. The primary sector is also called the agriculture and related sector. The industrial sector is another name for the secondary sector, and the service sector for the tertiary sector; "unorganised" is a different classification (conditions of work).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is **NOT** a tertiary-sector activity?

options.text_md: A carpenter making tables in his workshop
A courier delivering parcels in Jaipur
A bank clerk opening savings accounts
A teacher taking online classes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A carpenter making tables in his workshop. Making tables turns wood into furniture, which is manufacturing (secondary). Courier delivery, banking and teaching are services (tertiary).

questions.stem_md: On what basis are economic activities divided into the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors?

options.text_md: Who owns the enterprise: the government or private persons
Whether jobs are regular and protected by law
The number of workers each enterprise employs
The nature of the activity: using natural resources, manufacturing, or providing services

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The nature of the activity: using natural resources, manufacturing, or providing services. The three-sector classification is based on the **nature of the activity**. Ownership is the basis of the public–private classification; job conditions are the basis of the organised–unorganised classification.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true, and R explains A: without services such as transport, storage, credit and trade, farm and factory goods could not reach buyers, so these sectors could not grow.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Clay (a natural product) is changed into pots by a manufacturing process, so this is a secondary activity, even though it is done at home and not in a factory.

questions.stem_md: Activities in which natural products are changed into other forms through manufacturing belong to the ___ sector.
questions.solution_md: Manufacturing activities form the secondary (industrial) sector.

A rice mill removing husk and polishing grain

questions.solution_md: Trace one product through all three sectors and show the dependence in each direction; end with what happens if one link breaks.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Primary depends on secondary and tertiary:** a sugarcane farmer in Uttar Pradesh sells cane to a **sugar mill** and needs **transport and credit**.
2. **Secondary depends on primary:** the mill cannot run without **cane** as raw material.
3. **Tertiary depends on both:** truckers, traders and banks earn by moving, selling and financing **cane and sugar**. If the cane crop fails, all three sectors suffer.

questions.stem_md: The Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of a country is the value of

options.text_md: all goods and services, including intermediate goods, produced in a year
all final goods and services produced within the country during a particular year
all goods that the country exports during a year
all goods and services produced by its citizens anywhere in the world

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** all final goods and services produced within the country during a particular year. GDP counts only **final** goods and services produced **within the country** in a year. Including intermediate goods would double count; exports are only a part of output; and output of citizens abroad is not produced within the country.

questions.stem_md: A factory in Meerut makes cricket bats. Which of the following is an **intermediate** good?

options.text_md: Willow wood bought by the factory to make the bats
A finished bat bought by a young player
A set of bats bought by a school for its team
A bat-repair service bought by a club player

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Willow wood bought by the factory to make the bats. Willow wood is used up in making the final good (the bat), so it is intermediate. Bats bought by users and a repair service bought by a player are final goods and services.

questions.stem_md: Why is the value of intermediate goods **not** added separately when GDP is calculated?

options.text_md: Intermediate goods are not produced within the country
Their value is already included in the value of the final goods, so adding it again would count it twice
Intermediate goods have no market value
Only services, not goods, are counted in GDP

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Their value is already included in the value of the final goods, so adding it again would count it twice. The price of a final good already covers the raw materials used in it. Adding them again would be double counting. Intermediate goods do have value and may be made in the country; GDP counts both goods and services.

questions.stem_md: In India today, which sector contributes the **largest share of GDP**?

options.text_md: Primary sector
Secondary sector
Tertiary sector
All three contribute about equally

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Tertiary sector. Over the past decades the tertiary sector has become the largest producing sector and now contributes more than half of India's GDP; the primary sector's share has fallen below one-fifth.

questions.stem_md: Which sector still provides work to the **largest share of India's workers**?

options.text_md: Secondary sector
Tertiary sector
Public sector
Primary sector

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Primary sector. Although its share of output has fallen, the primary sector (mainly agriculture) still employs the largest share of workers, a little under half. The public sector is an ownership category, not one of the three sectors.

questions.stem_md: Which situation best shows **disguised unemployment**?

options.text_md: A graduate has applied for many jobs but has no work at all
A factory worker loses his job when the factory closes down
A woman works in a government office for eight hours a day with paid leave
Five brothers work on a small family plot that needs only two workers; output would not fall if three left

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Five brothers work on a small family plot that needs only two workers; output would not fall if three left. In disguised unemployment people **seem** to be working, but some are not needed: removing them does not reduce output. Having no work at all is open unemployment, losing a job when a factory closes is job loss, and the office worker is fully employed.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is **NOT** a reason for the growing importance of the tertiary sector in India?

options.text_md: Rising incomes increase demand for services such as eating out, tourism and private hospitals
Growth of farming and industry needs more transport, storage and trade
The primary sector has stopped producing goods
New services based on information and communication technology have grown fast

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The primary sector has stopped producing goods. The primary sector still produces large quantities of goods; only its **share** of GDP has fallen. The other three are genuine reasons: demand from rising incomes, support services for other sectors, and new IT-based services.

questions.stem_md: In the history of today's developed countries, which sector became the most important **after** the primary sector?

options.text_md: Tertiary sector
Secondary sector
Public sector
Unorganised sector

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Secondary sector. As new methods of production spread, factories grew and manufacturing (the secondary sector) became the most important; only later did services take over. Public and unorganised are other classifications.

questions.stem_md:
Read the statements about India.

I. The tertiary sector's share of GDP has risen over the decades.
II. The tertiary sector's share of employment has risen just as much as its share of GDP.
III. The primary sector still employs the largest share of workers.

Which of these are correct?

options.text_md: I and III only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** I and III only. Statement I is correct. Statement II is wrong: the tertiary sector's share of jobs has grown much less than its share of output. Statement III is correct. So only I and III.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The share of the tertiary sector in India's GDP has risen.

**Reason (R):** The tertiary sector also includes many low-paid workers such as small shopkeepers, street vendors and repair persons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true. But R does not explain why the share of the sector in GDP has risen (rising demand for services, support for other sectors and new IT services do). R is a separate fact about who works in the sector.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In disguised unemployment, people appear to be employed.

**Reason (R):** Removing the extra workers in disguised unemployment reduces total output sharply.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: all members seem busy on the farm. R is false: the defining feature is that output does **not** fall when the extra workers are removed.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** GDP counts only final goods and services.

**Reason (R):** Counting intermediate goods separately would lead to double counting.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R is the reason for A: the value of the final good already includes the inputs.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The value of the flour bought by a bakery is added to GDP separately from the value of the bread it sells.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Flour used by the bakery is an intermediate good. Its value is already inside the price of the bread, so adding it separately would count it twice.

questions.stem_md: The value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year is called its ___.
questions.solution_md: This is the definition of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

questions.stem_md: When more people are working on a task than are actually needed, so that some could leave without any fall in output, the situation is called ___ unemployment.
questions.solution_md: This is disguised (hidden) unemployment: the surplus workers look employed.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the stages through which the most important sector changed in today's developed countries, from earliest to latest.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Primary activities came first; surplus food freed people for crafts and trade; industrialisation made the secondary sector most important; finally the tertiary sector took the lead.

GDP is the value of final output of a year; cement used by a builder is used up in making the house; six workers where three are enough shows hidden surplus labour; the right to 100 days of work for rural households comes from MGNREGA 2005.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined chain, a farmer sells wheat worth ₹800 to a flour mill. The mill sells the flour for ₹1,200 to a bakery. The bakery sells bread worth ₹2,000 to consumers. By how much does this chain add to GDP (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Only the final good, the bread sold to consumers, is counted: ₹2,000.
Step 2: Check by value added: farmer ₹800 + mill (1,200 − 800) ₹400 + bakery (2,000 − 1,200) ₹800 = ₹2,000.
Step 3: Adding 800 + 1,200 + 2,000 = ₹4,000 would count the wheat and flour twice. Answer: ₹2,000.

marking_scheme.step: Counts only the final good (or adds value added at each stage)

questions.stem_md: In an imagined family in Bihar, seven members work on their 2-hectare farm. An agriculture officer finds that four of them could produce exactly the same output. How many members are disguisedly unemployed?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Workers needed for the same output = 4.
Step 2: Surplus workers = 7 − 4 = 3.
Step 3: These 3 members look busy but add nothing to output, so 3 are disguisedly unemployed.

questions.stem_md: An imagined country's GDP in a year is ₹50 lakh crore, of which the tertiary sector produces ₹27 lakh crore. What is the tertiary sector's share of GDP, in per cent?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Share = (tertiary output ÷ GDP) × 100.
Step 2: (27 ÷ 50) × 100 = 0.54 × 100 = 54.
Step 3: The tertiary sector produces 54% of GDP, more than half.

questions.stem_md: What are final goods? Why does GDP count only final goods and services?
questions.solution_md: Define final goods with an example, then give the double-counting reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Final goods** reach the **consumer** and are not used up in making other goods, e.g. a bicycle bought by a student.
2. Their price already **includes the value of intermediate goods**, so counting both would be **double counting**.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning of final goods with an example

questions.stem_md: Explain disguised unemployment with an example from rural India.
questions.solution_md: Give the meaning (surplus workers who appear employed) and an example where removing them leaves output unchanged.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. In **disguised unemployment** more people work on a task than are needed, so they **appear employed**.
2. E.g., six members of a family in Odisha work on a small plot that needs three; if three leave, **output does not fall**.

questions.stem_md: Give two examples of underemployment in towns and cities.
questions.solution_md: Each example must show people working below their capacity (few days of work, or long hours with very little output or income).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Casual workers** such as painters and plumbers in a city find paid work only on **some days** of the week.
2. A **street vendor** spends the whole day at her cart but earns little because she has **too few customers** for her time.

marking_scheme.step: First urban example of working below capacity

questions.stem_md: Explain three reasons why the tertiary sector has become the largest producing sector in India.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct reasons, each linked to more demand for services: basic public services, services that support other sectors, and demand from higher incomes plus IT.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Basic services**: a country needs hospitals, schools, post offices, police, courts and banks, which are mainly services.
2. **Support for other sectors**: growth of farming and industry needs **transport, storage, trade and credit**.
3. **Rising incomes and new technology**: richer people demand eating out, tourism and private schools, and **IT-based services** have grown fast.

marking_scheme.step: Support for primary and secondary sectors
Rising incomes or new IT-based services

questions.stem_md: Not every part of the tertiary sector is growing equally. Explain this statement.
questions.solution_md: Contrast the fast-growing modern services with the many low-paid, insecure service workers, and draw the conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **High-skill services** such as software, finance and telecom have grown fast and employ well-educated, well-paid workers.
2. A large number of tertiary workers are **small shopkeepers, vendors, repair persons and transport workers** who earn little and have no job security.
3. They are in services only because there are **no better jobs**; so the sector's growth has not improved everyone's life.

questions.stem_md: The tertiary sector produces more than half of India's GDP, but it employs less than a third of the workers. What problem does this show, and why has it happened?
questions.solution_md: Compare the shares of output and employment, explain why jobs lag (too few jobs created, skill needs), and state the result (underemployment in agriculture).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Jobs have **not shifted** out of agriculture as fast as **production** has; more than two-fifths of workers still depend on the primary sector.
2. The secondary and tertiary sectors have **not created enough jobs**, and many new service jobs need **skills and education**.
3. So many farm workers remain **underemployed**, with low incomes.

marking_scheme.step: Mismatch of output and employment shares identified
Reason: too few or skill-demanding jobs created
Result: underemployment in the primary sector

questions.stem_md: Describe how the importance of the three sectors has changed over time in developed countries. How is India's experience similar and how is it different?
questions.solution_md: Three stages for developed countries, then one similarity (output) and one difference (employment) for India.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Early stage:** in today's developed countries most people worked in the **primary sector**: farming, herding and fishing.
2. **Industrial stage:** better farming freed workers; with new methods, **factories** spread and the **secondary sector** became most important in output and jobs.
3. **Service stage:** over the last century the **tertiary sector** became the largest in both **production and employment**.
4. **India — similar:** our **output** has also shifted; the tertiary sector now produces **more than half of GDP**, and the primary sector less than a fifth.
5. **India — different:** **jobs have not shifted** as much; the primary sector still employs the **largest share** of workers, so many remain underemployed.

marking_scheme.step: Tertiary stage in output and employment

questions.stem_md: What is disguised unemployment? Why is it common in Indian agriculture? Suggest ways to reduce it.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, two reasons it is widespread in agriculture, and two kinds of remedies (more farm work; non-farm work).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Meaning:** more people work on a task than needed; they **appear employed**, but if some leave, **output does not fall**.
2. **Why common:** most farm families own **small plots**, and members have **no other work nearby**, so all of them work on the family land.
3. **Why common (2):** the secondary and tertiary sectors have **not created enough jobs** in rural areas.
4. **Remedy — farm side:** **irrigation** and better seeds allow a second crop, so more labour is truly needed.
5. **Remedy — off-farm jobs:** **food-processing units**, cold storage, rural roads, tourism and **MGNREGA** works give surplus workers paid work.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: small plots, no other work
Reason: other sectors have not created enough jobs
Remedy: irrigation or a second crop

questions.stem_md:
Study the table of an **imagined state, Ranipur**, and answer: compare the changes in each sector's share of output and of employment between 2000 and 2025, explain what the figures show, and suggest one way to deal with the problem they reveal.

| Sector | Share of state output, 2000 (%) | Share of state output, 2025 (%) | Share of workers, 2000 (%) | Share of workers, 2025 (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Primary | 38 | 17 | 62 | 47 |
| Secondary | 24 | 29 | 15 | 24 |
| Tertiary | 38 | 54 | 23 | 29 |

*(Imagined figures written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md: Read both pairs of columns, compare changes (38 → 17 and 38 → 54 for output; 62 → 47 and 23 → 29 for workers), divide the reading into what fell and what rose, interpret the low output per worker, and give one remedy.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Output:** the primary share **fell from 38% to 17%**, while the tertiary share **rose from 38% to 54%**, now more than half.
2. **Employment:** the primary share of workers fell **only from 62% to 47%**; the tertiary share rose **only from 23% to 29%**.
3. **Meaning:** in 2025, **47% of workers produce only 17% of output** in the primary sector, so output per worker there is very low.
4. This shows **disguised unemployment and underemployment** in agriculture: jobs have **not shifted** as fast as production.
5. **Suggestion:** create **rural non-farm jobs**, e.g. food-processing units and cold storage near farms, with skill training.

marking_scheme.step: Change in output shares with figures
Change in employment shares with figures
Interpretation: low output per worker in the primary sector
Names the problem: disguised unemployment / underemployment

questions.stem_md: Under MGNREGA 2005, how many days of wage employment in a year are guaranteed to a rural household whose adult members ask for work?

options.text_md: 50 days
100 days
200 days
365 days

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 100 days. The Act guarantees 100 days of unskilled manual work in a financial year to every rural household that demands it.

questions.stem_md: Under MGNREGA, if the government fails to provide work within 15 days of an application, the applicant

options.text_md: loses the right to apply again that year
must find work in the private sector
is given a permanent government job
is entitled to an unemployment allowance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** is entitled to an unemployment allowance. The guarantee is a legal right: if work is not provided within 15 days, the applicant gets an unemployment allowance. The other options contradict the Act.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined village of Vidarbha, farmers grow only one rain-fed crop a year and are idle for months. Which step would most directly create more work **in the village itself**?

options.text_md: Building check dams and small canals so that a second crop can be grown
Opening a shopping mall in the state capital
Giving each family a one-time cash gift
Moving the village's weekly market to the city

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Building check dams and small canals so that a second crop can be grown. Irrigation allows a second crop, so farm families and labourers get work for more months of the year in the village. A mall far away, a one-time gift or moving the market does not create lasting local work.

questions.stem_md: Under MGNREGA 2005, at least what share of the people given work should be women?

options.text_md: One-half
One-fourth
One-third
Two-thirds

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** One-third. The Act gives priority to women so that at least one-third of the beneficiaries are women.

questions.stem_md: Why is MGNREGA 2005 described as implementing the **right to work**?

options.text_md: It gives every citizen a permanent job in a government office
It is a charity programme that officials may stop at any time
Rural households can legally demand work, and if it is not given they receive an allowance
It guarantees jobs only to graduates in cities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Rural households can legally demand work, and if it is not given they receive an allowance. Work under MGNREGA is a legal entitlement that can be demanded, backed by the unemployment allowance. It is not a permanent job, not a discretionary charity, and it is for rural households doing unskilled manual work.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** MGNREGA 2005 guarantees 100 days of work to every unemployed person living in a city.

**Reason (R):** MGNREGA aims to provide wage employment to households in rural areas.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the guarantee is for **rural households**, not for individuals in cities. R is true.

questions.stem_md: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was passed by Parliament in the year ___.
questions.solution_md: The Act was passed in 2005 (as NREGA; "Mahatma Gandhi" was added to its name in 2009).

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps by which a rural household gets work under MGNREGA, in the correct order.

options.text_md: Wages are paid into the worker's bank or post-office account
Work is provided within 15 days of the application (or an unemployment allowance is due)
An adult member applies for work
The household registers with the gram panchayat and receives a job card

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). Registration and a job card come first, then the application for work, then work within 15 days, and finally payment of wages into an account.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: An imagined household in Jharkhand has already received 58 days of work under MGNREGA 2005 in the current financial year. For how many more days can it still demand work this year under the Act's guarantee?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Guarantee = 100 days per household per financial year.
Step 2: Days left = 100 − 58 = 42 days.

questions.stem_md: State any two features of MGNREGA 2005.
questions.solution_md: Any two correct provisions: 100 days, rural households, unemployment allowance, priority to women, works that improve land and water.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Every **rural household** is guaranteed **100 days** of unskilled manual work in a year.
2. If work is not given within **15 days**, an **unemployment allowance** is paid. (Also: at least one-third of workers are women.)

questions.stem_md: How can better rural roads and storage facilities create employment in villages?
questions.solution_md: Link each facility to new activities and the jobs they create.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Roads** let farmers send produce to bigger markets and create work for **truck drivers, loaders and traders**.
2. **Cold storage and godowns** let farmers store crops and sell later, and employ **workers, managers and technicians**.

marking_scheme.step: Roads and the jobs they create
Storage and the jobs it creates

questions.stem_md: Suggest three ways in which more employment can be created in a semi-rural area such as a small town surrounded by farms.
questions.solution_md: Three different, realistic sources of work tied to the area (processing, credit for small enterprises, local services).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Agro-processing**: set up units for pickles, rice milling or fruit juice using local crops.
2. **Cheap credit**: bank and SHG loans let people start **small shops, dairies or workshops**.
3. **Services**: expand **schools, health centres, tourism** and repair work, which need local workers.

questions.stem_md: How does MGNREGA help both rural households and the village economy? Give three points.
questions.solution_md: One benefit to households, one to land productivity, one to the wider village economy or women.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Households** get a guaranteed **income** in the lean season, which reduces hunger and distress migration.
2. Works such as **ponds, check dams and tree planting** build assets that raise **farm output** for years.
3. Wages are **spent locally**, which helps village shops and other workers; and **women** gain paid work and some independence.

marking_scheme.step: Wider benefit: local spending or women's work

questions.stem_md: MGNREGA 2005 is often called a law that implements the "right to work". Explain its main features and evaluate how far it helps rural people.
questions.solution_md: Two points on features, one on the kind of works, then a balanced judgement: benefits and limitations.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Guarantee:** every **rural household** can demand **100 days** of unskilled manual work in a year.
2. **Legal right:** if work is not given within **15 days**, an **unemployment allowance** is due; at least **one-third** of workers are **women**.
3. **Useful works:** priority to **water conservation, land development and rural roads**, which raise future output.
4. **Helps:** it gives income in the **lean season**, reduces **distress migration**, and payments into **bank accounts** reduce cheating.
5. **Limits:** **delayed wages**, fewer days than promised in many districts and weak works reduce its benefit; with timely payment and **social audits**, it works far better.

marking_scheme.step: Legal right: allowance; priority to women
Kind of works and why they matter

questions.stem_md: Read the source and answer the questions that follow. *(Illustrative source written by SOYL for practice; the people and places in it are imagined.)*

**(a)** Rural works chosen by the gram sabha, with wages for manual work, point to the 2005 employment guarantee Act.

**(b)** Look for an asset that changed farming: the check dam made a winter crop possible.

**(c) (i)** Connect the new asset to more months of farm work, and then to the end of seasonal migration.

**OR (c) (ii)** Suggestions must address delays or accountability; any two workable steps.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **MGNREGA 2005** (the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act).

**(b)** After the **check dam**, the farmer's family can **grow wheat in winter** (a second crop).
